Authors: Steven L. Kleiman
Date: Fri Apr  1 14:37:52 2005

We develop in detail most of the theory of the Picard scheme that Grothendieck sketched in two Bourbaki talks and in commentaries on them. Abelian Varieties - J.S. Milne   Top

pdf (current version 2.00)

An introduction to both the geometry and the arithmetic of abelian varieties. It includes a discussion of the theorems of Honda and Tate concerning abelian varieties over finite fields and the paper of Faltings in which he proves Mordell's Conjecture. Warning: These notes are less polished than the others.

### Contents

Introduction

#### Chapter I: Abelian Varieties: Geometry

  1. Definitions; basic properties.
  2. Abelian varieties over the complex numbers.
  3. Rational maps into abelian varieties.
  4. Review of cohomology.
  5. The theorem of the cube.
  6. Abelian varieties are projective.
  7. Isogenies
  8. The dual abelian variety
  9. The dual exact sequence.
  10. Endomorphisms.
  11. Polarizations and invertible sheaves.
  12. The etale cohomology of an abelian variety.
  13. Weil pairings.
  14. The Rosati involution.
  15. Geometric finiteness theorems.
  16. Families of abelian varieties.
  17. Neron models; semistable reduction.

STRONG FRANCHETTA CONJECTURE  3

# 1. Preliminaries

Let us collect some well-known facts on algebraic curves and their Picard schemes. Throughout this paper we fix an arbitrary ground field \(k\) of characteristic \(p \ge 0\). We will, however, also deal with algebraic schemes over extension fields \(k \subset F\). A curve over \(F\) is a proper 1-dimensional \(F\)-scheme \(X\) with \(F = H^0(X,\mathcal{O}_X)\). Each curve comes along with its Picard scheme \(\mathrm{Pic}_{X/F}\), which is a smooth group scheme of finite type. We denote by \(\mathrm{Pic}(X/F) = \mathrm{Pic}_{X/F}(F)\) its group of rational points. If \(X\) contains a rational point, this is nothing but the Picard group of \(X\). In general we have an exact sequence

\[
0 \longrightarrow \mathrm{Pic}(X) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Pic}(X/F) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Br}(F) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Br}(X),
\]

where \(\mathrm{Br}(F)\) is the Brauer group ([22], Corollary 5.3). Tsen’s Theorem implies the following (compare [22], Theorem 1.1):

**Lemma 1.1.** *Suppose that \(k\) is algebraically closed and that \(F\) is the function field of a smooth algebraic curve over \(k\). Then \(\mathrm{Pic}(X) = \mathrm{Pic}(X/F)\).*

Note that we do not loose rational points by passing to field extensions:

**Lemma 1.2.** *Let \(F \subset F'\) be a field extension, and \(X' = X \otimes_F F'\) the induced curve. Then the canonical map \(\mathrm{Pic}(X/F) \to \mathrm{Pic}(X'/F')\) is injective.*

*Proof.* We have \(\mathrm{Pic}_{X'/F'} = \mathrm{Pic}_{X/F} \otimes F'\), hence the fiber over the rational point \(0 \in \mathrm{Pic}_{X/F}\) is nothing but the rational point \(0 \in \mathrm{Pic}_{X'/F'}\).

Let \(\mathrm{Pic}^0_{X/F} \subset \mathrm{Pic}_{X/F}\) be the connected component of the origin. Equivalently, \(\mathrm{Pic}^0_{X/F}\) is the subgroup scheme given by numerically trivial line bundles. We sometimes write \(J = \mathrm{Pic}^0_{X/F}\) and call it the Jacobian of \(X\). If \(X\) is geometrically irreducible, the invertible sheaves of degree \(d\) comprise the other connected component \(\mathrm{Pic}^d_{X/F} \subset \mathrm{Pic}_{X/F}\). These are torsors under the group scheme \(\mathrm{Pic}^0_{X/F}\), in other words, elements of the Weil–Châtelet group \(H^1(k,\mathrm{Pic}^0_{X/F})\). Here cohomology is with respect to the fppf topology. However, étale cohomology gives the same result because \(\mathrm{Pic}^0_{X/F}\) is smooth ([22], Theorem 11.7). The torsor \(\mathrm{Pic}^d_{X/F}\) is trivial if and only if it contains a rational point. If \(\mathrm{Pic}^0_{X/F}\) is an abelian variety, \(\mathrm{Pic}^0(X/F)\) is also called the Mordell–Weil group.

Given an integer \(g \ge 3\), let \(M_g\) be the coarse moduli space of smooth curves of genus \(g\) over \(k\). Mumford [41] showed that this is an algebraic \(k\)-scheme. Moreover, Deligne and Mumford [8] proved that \(M_g\) is irreducible. If \(k\) is algebraically closed, its closed points correspond to isomorphism classes of smooth curves over \(k\). In any case, the coarse moduli space \(C = M_{g,1}\) of pointed smooth curves defines a tautological family of curves \(C \to M_g\).

We call \(C_\eta\) the generic curve of genus \(g\), where \(\eta \in M_g\) is the generic point. This is justified as follows: Let \(\overline{F}\) be an algebraic closure of the function field \(F = \kappa(\eta)\), and \(\overline{X}\) a smooth curve of genus \(g\) over \(\overline{F}\) corresponding to the geometric point \(\mathrm{Spec}(\overline{K}) \to M_g\). Then \(C_\eta \otimes_F \overline{F} \cong \overline{X}/\mathrm{Aut}(\overline{X})\). However, the generic curve of genus \(g \ge 3\) has trivial automorphism group [see [43] for an algebraic proof]. So the generic curve \(C_\eta\) is indeed a smooth curve of genus \(g\) over the function field \(F = \kappa(\eta)\). In contrast, the generic curve in genus two is the the projective line.

Title: The strong Franchetta Conjecture in arbitrary characteristics
Authors: Stefan Schroeer
Date: Tue Mar 19 06:33:11 2002

Using Moriwaki's calculation of the Q-Picard group for the moduli space of curves, I prove the strong Franchetta Conjecture in all characteristics. That is, the canonical class generates the group of rational points on the Picard scheme for the generic curve of genus g>2. Similar results hold for generic pointed curves. Moreover, I show that Hilbert's Irreducibility Theorem implies that there are many other nonclosed points in the moduli space of curves with such properties.
